steps.text: A system of linear equations consists of several equations with several unknowns that must ALL hold at the same time. Solving such systems is the heart of linear algebra – and in this chapter you lay the foundation.
steps.explanation:
Our roadmap:
1. What a system means geometrically
2. Three solution methods for small systems
3. Gaussian elimination for larger systems
4. When a system has no, one or infinitely many solutions
5. Word problems
steps.section: Chapter 1 · What is a system of equations?
steps.insight: All methods follow the same idea: transform the equations so that the solution set stays the same but the system becomes simpler.

steps.text: Every linear equation with two unknowns describes a line in the plane. A system of two equations therefore asks: where do two lines intersect?
steps.explanation:
The animation shows all three possible cases:
• The lines intersect in exactly one point: exactly one solution (here \((2, 1)\)).
• The lines are parallel and distinct: no solution.
• The lines coincide: infinitely many solutions (every point of the line).

There is nothing else: a linear system has either no, exactly one or infinitely many solutions – never exactly two.
steps.section: Chapter 1 · What is a system of equations?
steps.insight: It stays the same with three unknowns: three planes in space can meet in a point, a line, not at all, or in a whole plane.

steps.text: Method 1 – substitution: solve one equation for one variable and substitute the result into the other equation.
steps.explanation:
Substituting turns two equations with two unknowns into one equation with one unknown.

Important: use brackets! \(x - (3 - x)\) is \(x - 3 + x\), not \(x - 3 - x\).

Equating is a special case: if both equations are solved for the same variable (\(y = 2x - 1\) and \(y = -x + 5\)), set the right-hand sides equal: \(2x - 1 = -x + 5\).
steps.insight: Substitution pays off when a variable is almost free already (coefficient \(1\) or \(-1\)).

steps.text: Method 2 – elimination: scale the equations so that one variable cancels when adding.
steps.explanation:
The second equation is multiplied by \(3\) so that \(+3y\) and \(-3y\) cancel when added. Then substitute \(x = 3\) into one of the original equations: \(2 \cdot 3 + 3y = 12 \Rightarrow y = 2\).

Check in BOTH equations: \(4 \cdot 3 - 2 = 10\) ✓ and \(2 \cdot 3 + 3 \cdot 2 = 12\) ✓.

The elimination method is the basis of Gaussian elimination.
steps.insight: Permitted operations: multiply an equation by a number \(\neq 0\), and add a multiple of one equation to another. The solution set stays the same.

steps.text: What happens when a "strange" equation appears during the calculation?
steps.explanation:
Subtracting twice the first equation from the second gives:
• \(0 = 2\) – a false statement. The system has no solution (the lines are parallel).
• \(0 = 0\) – an always-true statement. The second equation contains no new information (the lines are identical). The solutions are all points \((3 - t, t)\) with \(t \in \mathbb{R}\).
steps.insight: If \(0 = c\) with \(c \neq 0\) appears, the system is unsolvable. If \(0 = 0\) appears, a variable remains free.

steps.text: For three or more unknowns, Gaussian elimination is the standard tool. Idea: systematically eliminate variables until the system has "staircase form" – then solve from the bottom up.
steps.formula:
\begin{aligned}
x + y + z &= 6 \\
2x - y + z &= 3 \\
x + 2y - z &= 2
\end{aligned}
\quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad
\left(\begin{array}{ccc|c} 1 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\ 2 & -1 & 1 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 & -1 & 2 \end{array}\right)
steps.explanation:
On the right the same system appears as an augmented coefficient matrix: the columns belong to \(x, y, z\), the last column to the right-hand side. This saves writing the variables over and over.

Permitted row operations (they don't change the solution set):
• Swap two rows
• Multiply a row by a number \(\neq 0\)
• Add a multiple of one row to another
steps.insight: Goal: zeros below the diagonal ("row echelon form"). The first non-zero entry of each row is called the pivot.

steps.text: Step by step: first eliminate \(x\) from rows 2 and 3, then \(y\) from row 3.
steps.explanation:
The last row says \(-7z = -21\), so \(z = 3\).

Back substitution:
• Row 2: \(y - 2z = -4 \Rightarrow y = -4 + 6 = 2\)
• Row 1: \(x + y + z = 6 \Rightarrow x = 6 - 2 - 3 = 1\)

Solution: \((x, y, z) = (1, 2, 3)\). Check in all equations: \(1 + 2 + 3 = 6\) ✓, \(2 - 2 + 3 = 3\) ✓, \(1 + 4 - 3 = 2\) ✓.
steps.insight: Swap rows when the pivot is \(0\) or when it makes the numbers simpler. Gaussian elimination works for any size – that's exactly why computers use it.

steps.text: In Gaussian elimination you can read the solution behaviour from the finished staircase form:
steps.explanation:
Example for "infinitely many": \(x + y + z = 3\) and \(y - z = 1\) – only two equations for three unknowns.

Set the free variable \(z = t\) (parameter). Then \(y = 1 + t\) and \(x = 3 - y - z = 2 - 2t\). Solution set:
\(L = \{(2 - 2t,\ 1 + t,\ t) \mid t \in \mathbb{R}\}\) – a line in space.

Check: \(x + y + z = 2 - 2t + 1 + t + t = 3\) ✓ for every \(t\).
steps.insight: Number of free parameters = number of unknowns minus number of pivots. Later this is the connection between rank and dimension.

steps.text: If a parameter is in the system, it decides the solution behaviour. Example: for which \(a\) is the system uniquely solvable?
steps.explanation:
• \(a \neq 2\): we may divide by \(a - 2\): \(y = 0\), \(x = 1\). Exactly one solution.
• \(a = 2\): the equation becomes \(0 \cdot y = 0\) – always true. Infinitely many solutions \((1 - t, t)\).

Again: you may only divide by an expression containing a parameter if it is \(\neq 0\) – hence the case distinction.
steps.insight: For parameter problems always look for the critical value (here \(a = 2\)) where the pivot vanishes, and examine this case separately.

steps.text: Word problems: name the unknowns from the text, set up an equation for every statement, solve the system, check the result in context.
steps.explanation:
Example: "3 apples and 2 pears cost €4.80, 2 apples and 5 pears cost €7.60."

Elimination: first equation times \(5\), second times \(2\): \(15a + 10b = 24\) and \(4a + 10b = 15.2\). Subtract: \(11a = 8.8\), so \(a = 0.8\). Then \(b = (4.8 - 2.4) : 2 = 1.2\).

Check against the text: \(3 \cdot 0.8 + 2 \cdot 1.2 = 4.8\) ✓, \(2 \cdot 0.8 + 5 \cdot 1.2 = 7.6\) ✓.
steps.insight: Always define first what \(x\) and \(y\) mean – including the unit.

steps.text: Look back at what you can do now:
steps.explanation:
1. Two equations with two unknowns = two lines: one intersection point, none or infinitely many.

2. Substitution, equating, elimination. Check in BOTH equations.

3. Gaussian elimination: augmented matrix, row operations, echelon form, back substitution.

4. \(0 = c\) (\(c \neq 0\)): unsolvable. Free variable: infinitely many solutions with a parameter.

5. Parameter problems: find the critical value and separate the cases.
steps.insight: Congratulations! In linear algebra everything returns: matrices, rank, determinants and the solvability of linear systems. You can use the matrix calculator in the app to check your work.
